subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In a drainage basin, what is the 'watershed'?
options: The point where two rivers join together
The imaginary boundary line separating one drainage basin from another
The place where a river begins
The point where the river enters the sea
questions.explain: The watershed is the ridge of high land that marks the edge of a drainage basin and separates it from neighbouring basins.

questions.q: What term describes the point where a tributary joins the main river?
questions.explain: A confluence is the location where two rivers or a tributary and the main channel meet.

questions.q: Which erosion process makes transported rocks smaller and rounder as they collide with one another?
questions.explain: Attrition is the wearing down and rounding of load particles as they knock against each other during transport.

questions.q: A river carries dissolved minerals from areas of soluble rock such as chalk. Which method of transportation is this?
questions.explain: In solution, soluble material is dissolved and carried invisibly within the water.

questions.q: River discharge is measured in cumecs. What does a cumec represent?
questions.explain: Discharge is the volume of water passing a point per second, so a cumec is one cubic metre per second (m3/s).

questions.q: During a flood, the sheer force of fast-flowing water forces air into cracks in the river bank, weakening it. Which process is this?
questions.explain: Hydraulic action is erosion caused by the force of the water alone, compressing air in cracks and breaking rock apart.

questions.q: Why does the average velocity of a river generally increase towards its mouth despite the gentler gradient?
options: There is more friction from a rough, boulder-strewn bed
The channel becomes deeper and smoother, reducing friction
The river loses water to evaporation
questions.explain: Downstream the channel is larger and smoother, so proportionally less water touches the bed and banks, reducing friction and increasing efficiency and velocity.

questions.q: What is the name of the deep hollow eroded at the base of a waterfall?
questions.explain: The falling water and abrasion of rocks erode a deep plunge pool at the foot of the waterfall.

questions.q: How does a gorge typically form below a waterfall?
options: Deposition builds up ridges over many years
The waterfall retreats upstream as it collapses repeatedly, leaving a steep-sided valley
A meander is cut off during a flood
questions.explain: As the soft rock is undercut and the overhang of hard rock collapses, the waterfall retreats upstream, leaving behind a steep-sided gorge.

questions.q: On a meander, where is the fastest flow and greatest erosion found?
options: On the inner bank, forming a slip-off slope
On the outer bank, forming a river cliff
In the centre of the channel only
questions.explain: The fastest current swings to the outer bend, causing erosion and a steep river cliff, while deposition occurs on the slower inner bank.

questions.q: What gently sloping feature is formed by deposition on the inner bank of a meander?
questions.explain: Where flow is slowest on the inner bend, sediment is deposited to build a gently sloping slip-off slope (point bar).

questions.q: Which sequence best describes the formation of an ox-bow lake?
options: Deposition seals a channel, then erosion reopens it
Erosion narrows the meander neck until the river cuts across it, then deposition seals off the old loop
A waterfall retreats until it becomes a lake
Levees burst and flood a floodplain permanently
questions.explain: Continued erosion narrows the meander neck; during a flood the river breaks through, and deposition then cuts off the abandoned loop to leave an ox-bow lake.

questions.q: What are levees?
options: Deep pools at the base of waterfalls
Raised banks of sediment along the sides of a river channel
Artificial channels dug to divert floodwater
questions.explain: Levees are natural raised embankments formed when a river deposits its coarsest load along its banks during repeated floods.

questions.q: Why is a floodplain usually a flat area of very fertile land?
options: It is scoured by vertical erosion in the upper course
Repeated floods deposit layers of fine, nutrient-rich alluvium
Levees prevent any deposition from occurring
It is formed entirely by hydraulic action
questions.explain: When a river floods it spreads out and deposits fine alluvium across the valley floor, building a flat, fertile floodplain.

questions.q: On a flood (storm) hydrograph, what does 'lag time' measure?
options: The time between peak rainfall and peak discharge
The height of the peak discharge
The speed of the river at its mouth
questions.explain: Lag time is the delay between the peak of the rainfall and the peak discharge of the river.

questions.q: A drainage basin is urbanised with roads, roofs and drains replacing fields. What is the most likely effect on its storm hydrograph?
options: A longer lag time and lower peak discharge
A shorter lag time and higher peak discharge
No change to lag time or discharge
A gentler rising limb and gradual falling limb
questions.explain: Impermeable surfaces and drains speed water to the river, shortening lag time and raising peak discharge, creating a 'flashy' hydrograph and greater flood risk.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of soft engineering river management?
options: Building a concrete dam and reservoir
Constructing flood walls along the banks
questions.explain: Afforestation is a soft-engineering approach that works with natural processes, as trees intercept rainfall and slow runoff, unlike hard-engineering structures.

questions.q: A river channel has a cross-sectional area of 12 m2 and an average velocity of 3 m/s. What is its discharge?
questions.explain: Discharge = cross-sectional area x velocity = 12 x 3 = 36 cumecs (m3/s).

questions.q: A council wants a low-cost, environmentally friendly way to reduce flood risk in a rural valley with spare land. Which strategy best fits?
options: Building a large concrete dam across the valley
Designating washlands and zoning the floodplain for grazing not housing
Encasing the whole channel in concrete
Constructing high flood walls through the village
questions.explain: Floodplain zoning and washlands are cheap soft-engineering options that allow natural flooding on low-value land while protecting property.

questions.q: A river flows over a band of hard, resistant rock lying on top of softer rock. Which landform is most likely to develop here?
questions.explain: Where a river crosses hard rock overlying softer rock, the soft rock is undercut and eroded faster, creating a step in the long profile and a waterfall.
